claim: NAD+ participates in intracellular and extracellular signaling events unrelated to metabolism.
source: Nicotinamide adenine dinucleotide (NAD+) participates in intracellular and extracellular signaling events unrelated to metabolism.
evidence: This is a general statement supported by citations in the introduction section.

claim: In animals, purinergic receptors are required for extracellular NAD+ (eNAD+) to evoke biological responses.
source: In animals, purinergic receptors are required for extracellular NAD+ (eNAD+) to evoke biological responses, indicating that eNAD+ may be sensed by cell-surface receptors.
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to previous research on animal purinergic receptors.

claim: The identity of eNAD+-binding receptors remains elusive.
source: However, the identity of eNAD+-binding receptors still remains elusive.
evidence: This is a statement about the state of knowledge in the field prior to this study.

claim: LecRK-I.8 is a potential eNAD+ receptor in Arabidopsis.
source: Here, we identify a lectin receptor kinase (LecRK), LecRK-I.8, as a potential eNAD+ receptor in Arabidopsis.
evidence: This is the main claim of the paper, supported by multiple lines of experimental evidence presented throughout.

claim: The extracellular lectin domain of LecRK-I.8 binds NAD+ with a dissociation constant of 436.5 ± 104.8 nM.
source: The extracellular lectin domain of LecRK-I.8 binds NAD+ with a dissociation constant of 436.5 ± 104.8 nM, although much higher concentrations are needed to trigger in vivo responses.
evidence: This is directly supported by the saturation binding assay data shown in Figure 5E.

claim: Much higher concentrations of NAD+ are needed to trigger in vivo responses than the dissociation constant of LecRK-I.8.
source: The extracellular lectin domain of LecRK-I.8 binds NAD+ with a dissociation constant of 436.5 ± 104.8 nM, although much higher concentrations are needed to trigger in vivo responses.
evidence: This is supported by the observation that 5 μM NAD+ was needed to induce early defense genes (Figure 5—figure supplement 3).

claim: Mutations in LecRK-I.8 inhibit NAD+-induced immune responses.
source: Mutations in LecRK-I.8 inhibit NAD+-induced immune responses, whereas overexpression of LecRK-I.8 enhances the Arabidopsis response to NAD+.
evidence: This is supported by data in Figures 2A-D showing reduced PR gene expression and disease resistance in lecrk-I.8 mutants.

claim: Overexpression of LecRK-I.8 enhances the Arabidopsis response to NAD+.
source: Mutations in LecRK-I.8 inhibit NAD+-induced immune responses, whereas overexpression of LecRK-I.8 enhances the Arabidopsis response to NAD+.
evidence: This is supported by data in Figures 2E-G showing enhanced PR gene expression in 35S:LecRK-I.8 lines.

claim: LecRK-I.8 is required for basal resistance against bacterial pathogens.
source: Furthermore, LecRK-I.8 is required for basal resistance against bacterial pathogens, substantiating a role for eNAD+ in plant immunity.
evidence: This is supported by data in Figure 8 showing increased susceptibility of lecrk-I.8 mutants to Psm ES4326.

claim: Lectin receptors can potentially function as eNAD+-binding receptors.
source: Our results demonstrate that lectin receptors can potentially function as eNAD+-binding receptors and provide direct evidence for eNAD+ being an endogenous signaling molecule in plants.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the binding data and functional studies presented in the paper.

claim: eNAD+ is an endogenous signaling molecule in plants.
source: Our results demonstrate that lectin receptors can potentially function as eNAD+-binding receptors and provide direct evidence for eNAD+ being an endogenous signaling molecule in plants.
evidence: This is supported by the identification of a receptor, the role in basal immunity, and previous work showing NAD+ release during pathogen infection.

claim: NAD+ is the precursor of the second messenger cyclic ADP-ribose (cADPR).
source: NAD+ is the precursor of the second messenger cyclic ADP-ribose (cADPR), which triggers calcium (Ca2+) release from intracellular stores in various organisms (Galione and Churchill, 2000; Lee, 2001; Hunt et al., 2004; Ziegler, 2005).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by multiple citations.

claim: cADPR triggers calcium (Ca2+) release from intracellular stores in various organisms.
source: NAD+ is the precursor of the second messenger cyclic ADP-ribose (cADPR), which triggers calcium (Ca2+) release from intracellular stores in various organisms (Galione and Churchill, 2000; Lee, 2001; Hunt et al., 2004; Ziegler, 2005).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by multiple citations.

claim: NAD+ functions as the ADP-ribose donor in protein ADP-ribosylation reactions.
source: NAD+ also functions as the ADP-ribose donor and the acetyl group acceptor in protein ADP-ribosylation and deacetylation reactions, respectively (Jacobson and Jacobson, 1999; Bürkle, 2001; Denu, 2003; Jackson et al., 2003; Hunt et al., 2004).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by multiple citations.

claim: NAD+ functions as the acetyl group acceptor in protein deacetylation reactions.
source: NAD+ also functions as the ADP-ribose donor and the acetyl group acceptor in protein ADP-ribosylation and deacetylation reactions, respectively (Jacobson and Jacobson, 1999; Bürkle, 2001; Denu, 2003; Jackson et al., 2003; Hunt et al., 2004).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by multiple citations.

claim: Cellular NAD+ can be released into the extracellular space by active exocytosis or diffusion through transmembrane transporters in living cells.
source: In response to environmental stimuli, cellular NAD+ can also be released into the extracellular space by active exocytosis or diffusion through transmembrane transporters in living cells or passive leakage across membrane in collapsed tissues (Bruzzone et al., 2001; Contreras et al., 2003; Seman et al., 2003; Adriouch et al., 2007).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: Cellular NAD+ can be released into the extracellular space by passive leakage across membrane in collapsed tissues.
source: In response to environmental stimuli, cellular NAD+ can also be released into the extracellular space by active exocytosis or diffusion through transmembrane transporters in living cells or passive leakage across membrane in collapsed tissues (Bruzzone et al., 2001; Contreras et al., 2003; Seman et al., 2003; Adriouch et al., 2007).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: Extracellular NAD+ (eNAD+) plays an important signaling role in numerous physiological and pathological processes.
source: It has recently been shown that extracellular NAD+ (eNAD+) plays an important signaling role in numerous physiological and pathological processes (Billington et al., 2006; Haag et al., 2007; Adriouch et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: In animal cells, eNAD+ can be processed by ectoenzymes such as CD38, CD157, and mono(ADP-ribosyl)transferases (ARTs).
source: In animal cells, eNAD+ can be processed by ectoenzymes such as CD38, CD157, and mono(ADP-ribosyl)transferases (ARTs) (Billington et al., 2006).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous research.

claim: CD38 is a multifunctional enzyme attached to the extracellular surface of the plasma membrane.
source: CD38 is a multifunctional enzyme attached to the extracellular surface of the plasma membrane, which utilizes NAD+ as the substrate to produce cADPR (Ceni et al., 2003; De Flora et al., 2004; Krebs et al., 2005; Malavasi et al., 2006; Morabito et al., 2006; Partidá-Sánchez et al., 2007).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to previous research.

claim: CD38 utilizes NAD+ as the substrate to produce cADPR.
source: CD38 is a multifunctional enzyme attached to the extracellular surface of the plasma membrane, which utilizes NAD+ as the substrate to produce cADPR (Ceni et al., 2003; De Flora et al., 2004; Krebs et al., 2005; Malavasi et al., 2006; Morabito et al., 2006; Partidá-Sánchez et al., 2007).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to previous research.

claim: ARTs are glycosylphoshpatidylinositol-anchored or secreted ectoenzymes that use NAD+ to ADP-ribosylate lipid raft-associated signaling proteins.
source: ARTs are glycosylphoshpatidylinositol-anchored or secreted ectoenzymes that use NAD+ to ADP-ribosylate lipid raft-associated signaling proteins (Nemoto et al., 1996; Han et al., 2000; Seman et al., 2003; Bannas et al., 2005; Zolkiewska, 2005).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to previous research.

claim: NAD+ promotes intracellular [Ca2+] elevation in human purinoceptor P2Y11-transfected astrocytoma cells.
source: Moreschi et al. (2006) reported that NAD+ promotes intracellular [Ca2+] elevation in the human purinoceptor P2Y11-tranfected astrocytoma cells, but not in untransfected cells.
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Moreschi et al. (2006).

claim: Treatment with the selective and potent P2Y11 inhibitor NF157 prevents NAD+-induced intracellular [Ca2+] increases in human granulocytes.
source: They also showed that, in human granulocytes, treatment with the selective and potent P2Y11 inhibitor NF157 and down-regulation of P2Y11 expression by short interference RNA, both prevented NAD+-induced intracellular [Ca2+] increases and chemotaxis (Moreschi et al., 2006).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Moreschi et al. (2006).

claim: Down-regulation of P2Y11 expression by short interference RNA prevents NAD+-induced intracellular [Ca2+] increases in human granulocytes.
source: They also showed that, in human granulocytes, treatment with the selective and potent P2Y11 inhibitor NF157 and down-regulation of P2Y11 expression by short interference RNA, both prevented NAD+-induced intracellular [Ca2+] increases and chemotaxis (Moreschi et al., 2006).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Moreschi et al. (2006).

claim: P2Y11 is involved in eNAD+-triggered transmembrane signaling.
source: These results demonstrate that P2Y11 is involved in eNAD+-triggered transmembrane signaling.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the cited work of Moreschi et al. (2006).

claim: Purinoceptors, including P2Y1, P2X1, P2X4, and P2X7, are engaged in eNAD+-mediated signaling.
source: Several other studies using similar approaches have also indicated that purinoceptors, including P2Y1, P2X1, P2X4, and P2X7, are engaged in eNAD+-mediated signaling (Mutafova-Yambolieva et al., 2007; Grahnert et al., 2009; Klein et al., 2009).
evidence: This is supported by citations to multiple studies.

claim: NAD+ per se has never been demonstrated to bind to purinoceptors.
source: However, NAD+per se has never been demonstrated to bind to purinoceptors, and thus the identity of eNAD+ receptors still remains a mystery in animals.
evidence: This is a statement about the state of knowledge in the field.

claim: NAD+ and its derivatives function in stress tolerance and/or defense signaling in plants.
source: In plants, NAD+ and its derivatives have also been shown to function in stress tolerance and/or defense signaling (Dutilleul et al., 2005; Adams-Phillips et al., 2010; PetriacqPétriacq et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: Overexpression of the bacterial NAD+ biosynthesis gene nadC enhances defense gene expression and bacterial pathogen resistance.
source: Overexpression of the bacterial NAD+ biosynthesis gene nadC, which increases intracellular NAD+ levels, enhances defense gene expression and bacterial pathogen resistance (Pétriacq et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Pétriacq et al. (2012).

claim: Mutations in FLAGELLIN-INSENSITIVE4 suppress stomatal immunity.
source: In contrast, mutations in FLAGELLIN-INSENSITIVE4, a de novo NAD+ biosynthesis gene, suppress stomatal immunity (Macho et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Macho et al. (2012).

claim: Overexpression of Arabidopsis thaliana Nudix hydrolase homolog 6 (AtNUDT6) leads to alterations of intracellular NADH levels and salicylic acid (SA)-mediated defense signaling.
source: Furthermore, overexpression of Arabidopsis thaliana Nudix hydrolase homolog 6 (AtNUDT6), which encodes an ADP-ribose/NADH pyrophosphohydrolase, and knockout of AtNUDT6, AtNUDT7, or AtNUDT8 lead to alterations of intracellular NADH levels and salicylic acid (SA)-mediated defense signaling (Bartsch et al., 2006; Ge et al., 2007; Ishikawa et al., 2010; Fonseca and Dong, 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citations to multiple studies.

claim: Knockout of AtNUDT6, AtNUDT7, or AtNUDT8 leads to alterations of intracellular NADH levels and salicylic acid (SA)-mediated defense signaling.
source: Furthermore, overexpression of Arabidopsis thaliana Nudix hydrolase homolog 6 (AtNUDT6), which encodes an ADP-ribose/NADH pyrophosphohydrolase, and knockout of AtNUDT6, AtNUDT7, or AtNUDT8 lead to alterations of intracellular NADH levels and salicylic acid (SA)-mediated defense signaling (Bartsch et al., 2006; Ge et al., 2007; Ishikawa et al., 2010; Fonseca and Dong, 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citations to multiple studies.

claim: Exogenous NAD+ induces SA-dependent and -independent PATHOGENESIS-RELATED (PR) gene expression and disease resistance.
source: We have recently shown that exogenous NAD+ induces SA-dependent and -independent PATHOGENESIS-RELATED (PR) gene expression and disease resistance (Zhang and Mou, 2009).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Zhang and Mou (2009).

claim: Pathogen-induced hypersensitive response causes leakage of NAD+ into the extracellular fluid at concentrations sufficient to induce PR gene expression and disease resistance.
source: Importantly, we found that pathogen-induced hypersensitive response causes leakage of NAD+ into the extracellular fluid at concentrations sufficient to induce PR gene expression and disease resistance (Zhang and Mou, 2009).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Zhang and Mou (2009).

claim: Proteins with significant homology to animal CD38/CD157, ARTs, and purinoceptors are absent in plants.
source: However, since proteins with significant homology to animal CD38/CD157, ARTs, and purinoceptors are absent in plants, it remains unclear if eNAD+ is an endogenous signaling molecule in plants and if plants use similar mechanisms to process or perceive eNAD+ (Hunt et al., 2004; Sánchez et al., 2004; Zolkiewska, 2005; Zhang and Mou, 2008).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: Expression of the human NAD+-metabolizing ectoenzyme CD38 partially compromises systemic acquired resistance (SAR) in Arabidopsis.
source: We have shown that expression of the human NAD+-metabolizing ectoenzyme CD38 partially compromises systemic acquired resistance (SAR) in Arabidopsis (Zhang and Mou, 2012), which strongly suggests that plants may use different mechanisms to sense eNAD+.
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Zhang and Mou (2012).

claim: The Mediator complex subunits MED14/STRUWWELPETER and MED16/SENSITIVE TO FREEZING6/IEN1 function downstream of eNAD+.
source: Characterization of several ien mutants revealed that the Mediator complex subunits MED14/STRUWWELPETER and MED16/SENSITIVE TO FREEZING6 /IEN1 as well as the Elongator complex function downstream of eNAD+ (Zhang et al., 2012, 2013; An et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous work by the authors.

claim: The Elongator complex functions downstream of eNAD+.
source: Characterization of several ien mutants revealed that the Mediator complex subunits MED14/STRUWWELPETER and MED16/SENSITIVE TO FREEZING6 /IEN1 as well as the Elongator complex function downstream of eNAD+ (Zhang et al., 2012, 2013; An et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous work by the authors.

claim: NAD+ addition caused upregulation of 2155 genes and downregulation of 2014 genes compared to mock treatment.
source: Compared to the mock (water) treatment, NAD+ addition caused profound transcriptional changes, including upregulation of 2155 genes and downregulation of 2014 genes.
evidence: This is directly supported by the microarray data (GSE76568).

claim: Genes involved in plant immune responses were significantly enriched in the NAD+-upregulated genes.
source: In the upregulated genes, those involved in plant immune responses were significantly enriched, whereas in the downregulated genes, those associated with responses to hormone stimuli, such as auxin stimulus, were overrepresented (Figure 1A).
evidence: This is supported by Gene Ontology enrichment analysis shown in Figure 1A.

claim: Genes associated with responses to hormone stimuli, such as auxin stimulus, were overrepresented in the NAD+-downregulated genes.
source: In the upregulated genes, those involved in plant immune responses were significantly enriched, whereas in the downregulated genes, those associated with responses to hormone stimuli, such as auxin stimulus, were overrepresented (Figure 1A).
evidence: This is supported by Gene Ontology enrichment analysis shown in Figure 1A.

claim: The NAD+-upregulated genes include a large number of pathogen-associated molecular pattern (PAMP)-triggered immunity (PTI) and SA pathway genes.
source: The NAD+-upregulated genes include a large number of pathogen-associated molecular pattern (PAMP)-triggered immunity (PTI) and SA pathway genes (Supplementary file 1A).
evidence: This is supported by the supplementary data file.

claim: Expression of several jasmonic acid (JA)/ethylene (ET)-mediated defense pathway genes was suppressed by NAD+ treatment.
source: In contrast, expression of several jasmonic acid (JA)/ethylene (ET)-mediated defense pathway genes, including the widely used defense marker gene PLANT DEFENSIN1.2, was suppressed by NAD+ treatment (Supplementary file 1A).
evidence: This is supported by the supplementary data file.

claim: More than 88% of the NAD+-induced genes were also activated by the bacterial pathogen Pseudomonas syringae pv. tomato (Pst) DC3000 carrying the effector avrRpt2.
source: Interestingly, more than 88% of the NAD+-induced genes were also activated by the bacterial pathogen Pseudomonas syringae pv. tomato (Pst) DC3000 carrying the effector avrRpt2 (Figure 1B) (Wang et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by the Venn diagram in Figure 1B comparing NAD+-induced genes with pathogen-induced genes.

claim: NAD+-induced resistance to the bacterial pathogen P. syringae pv. maculicola (Psm) ES4326 was reduced in the Salk_066416 T-DNA insertion line.
source: We isolated transferred DNA (T-DNA) insertion lines for fourteen of the RK genes (Supplementary file 1B), tested their responsiveness to NAD+, and found that NAD+-induced resistance to the bacterial pathogen P. syringae pv. maculicola (Psm) ES4326 was reduced in one T-DNA insertion line (Arabidopsis Biological Resource Center accession code Salk_066416) (Figure 2—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This is supported by the data in Figure 2—figure supplement 1A.

claim: Salk_066416 carries a T-DNA insertion in the gene At5g60280, which encodes LecRK-I.8.
source: Salk_066416 carries a T-DNA insertion in the gene At5g60280, which was predicted to encode the legume-like (L-type) lectin receptor kinase-I.8 (LecRK-I.8) (Bouwmeester and Govers, 2009).
evidence: This is supported by the T-DNA insertion site information and citation to Bouwmeester and Govers (2009).

claim: The three T-DNA insertion lines (Salk_066416, Salk_005125, and Salk_206382) had reduced LecRK-I.8 transcript levels.
source: The three T-DNA insertion lines had reduced transcript levels (Figure 2—figure supplement 1B and C).
evidence: This is supported by the qPCR data in Figure 2—figure supplement 1C.

claim: The lecrk-I.8–4 mutant accumulated higher transcript levels than lecrk-I.8–2 and lecrk-I.8–3, and was considered a weak allele.
source: The lecrk-I.8–4 mutant accumulated higher transcript levels than lecrk-I.8–2 and lecrk-I.8–3, and was considered a weak allele (Figure 2—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: This is supported by the qPCR data in Figure 2—figure supplement 1C.

claim: NAD+-induced expression of PR1 was significantly inhibited in all three lecrk-I.8 alleles.
source: NAD+-induced expression of PR1 and resistance to Psm ES4326 were significantly inhibited in all three lecrk-I.8 alleles but not in the extracellular ATP (eATP) receptor mutant dorn1-3 (Choi et al., 2014), and induction of PR2 and PR5 was also repressed in lecrk-I.8–2 and lecrk-I.8–3 (Figure 2A–D).
evidence: This is supported by the qPCR data in Figure 2A.

claim: NAD+-induced resistance to Psm ES4326 was significantly inhibited in all three lecrk-I.8 alleles.
source: NAD+-induced expression of PR1 and resistance to Psm ES4326 were significantly inhibited in all three lecrk-I.8 alleles but not in the extracellular ATP (eATP) receptor mutant dorn1-3 (Choi et al., 2014), and induction of PR2 and PR5 was also repressed in lecrk-I.8–2 and lecrk-I.8–3 (Figure 2A–D).
evidence: This is supported by the bacterial growth data in Figure 2D.

claim: NAD+-induced expression of PR1 was not inhibited in the extracellular ATP (eATP) receptor mutant dorn1-3.
source: NAD+-induced expression of PR1 and resistance to Psm ES4326 were significantly inhibited in all three lecrk-I.8 alleles but not in the extracellular ATP (eATP) receptor mutant dorn1-3 (Choi et al., 2014), and induction of PR2 and PR5 was also repressed in lecrk-I.8–2 and lecrk-I.8–3 (Figure 2A–D).
evidence: This is supported by the qPCR data in Figure 2A.

claim: Induction of PR2 and PR5 was repressed in lecrk-I.8–2 and lecrk-I.8–3.
source: NAD+-induced expression of PR1 and resistance to Psm ES4326 were significantly inhibited in all three lecrk-I.8 alleles but not in the extracellular ATP (eATP) receptor mutant dorn1-3 (Choi et al., 2014), and induction of PR2 and PR5 was also repressed in lecrk-I.8–2 and lecrk-I.8–3 (Figure 2A–D).
evidence: This is supported by the qPCR data in Figures 2B and 2C.

claim: LecRK-I.8 is a component of the eNAD+-induced defense signaling pathway.
source: These results indicate that LecRK-I.8 is a component of the eNAD+-induced defense signaling pathway.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the data showing reduced NAD+ responses in lecrk-I.8 mutants.

claim: Induction of PR2 and PR5 was significantly enhanced in the dorn1-3 mutant.
source: Interestingly, induction of PR2 and PR5 was significantly enhanced in the dorn1-3 mutant (Figure 2B and C), which is consistent with eATP being a negative regulator of SA signaling (Chivasa et al., 2009).
evidence: This is supported by the qPCR data in Figures 2B and 2C.

claim: eATP is a negative regulator of SA signaling.
source: Interestingly, induction of PR2 and PR5 was significantly enhanced in the dorn1-3 mutant (Figure 2B and C), which is consistent with eATP being a negative regulator of SA signaling (Chivasa et al., 2009).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Chivasa et al. (2009).

claim: NAD+-induced expression of PR1 and PR5 in 35S:LecRK-I.8 transgenic lines was significantly enhanced.
source: Nevertheless, although the transgenic lines, which expressed higher levels of LecRK-I.8 than the wild type, did not show enhanced disease resistance (Figure 2—figure supplement 2B), NAD+-induced expression of PR1 and PR5 in these lines was significantly enhanced (Figure 2E–2G).
evidence: This is supported by the qPCR data in Figures 2F and 2G.

claim: 35S:LecRK-I.8 transgenic lines expressing higher levels of LecRK-I.8 than the wild type did not show enhanced disease resistance.
source: Nevertheless, although the transgenic lines, which expressed higher levels of LecRK-I.8 than the wild type, did not show enhanced disease resistance (Figure 2—figure supplement 2B), NAD+-induced expression of PR1 and PR5 in these lines was significantly enhanced (Figure 2E–2G).
evidence: This is supported by the bacterial growth data in Figure 2—figure supplement 2B.

claim: Both DORN1 and LecRK-I.8 contain a putative transmembrane domain.
source: Both DORN1 and LecRK-I.8 contain a putative transmembrane domain and two putative arginine-glycine-aspartic acid (RGD)-binding motifs that likely mediate plant cell wall-plasma membrane interactions (Gouget et al., 2006) (Figure 3A and Figure 3—figure supplement 1), suggesting their possible plasma membrane localization.
evidence: This is supported by sequence analysis shown in Figure 3A and Figure 3—figure supplement 1.

claim: Both DORN1 and LecRK-I.8 contain two putative arginine-glycine-aspartic acid (RGD)-binding motifs.
source: Both DORN1 and LecRK-I.8 contain a putative transmembrane domain and two putative arginine-glycine-aspartic acid (RGD)-binding motifs that likely mediate plant cell wall-plasma membrane interactions (Gouget et al., 2006) (Figure 3A and Figure 3—figure supplement 1), suggesting their possible plasma membrane localization.
evidence: This is supported by sequence analysis shown in Figure 3A.

claim: RGD-binding motifs likely mediate plant cell wall-plasma membrane interactions.
source: Both DORN1 and LecRK-I.8 contain a putative transmembrane domain and two putative arginine-glycine-aspartic acid (RGD)-binding motifs that likely mediate plant cell wall-plasma membrane interactions (Gouget et al., 2006) (Figure 3A and Figure 3—figure supplement 1), suggesting their possible plasma membrane localization.
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Gouget et al. (2006).

claim: DORN1 is localized in the plasma membrane.
source: Indeed, DORN1 has been shown to be localized in the plasma membrane (Bouwmeester et al., 2011).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Bouwmeester et al. (2011).

claim: LecRK-I.8-GFP is localized at the plasma membrane.
source: As shown in Figure 3C, the GFP and mCherry signals in the co-transformed N. benthamiana epidermal cell precisely overlapped with each other. Since AHA2 encodes a well-established plasma membrane localized P-type H+- ATPase (DeWitt et al., 1996), this result indicates that LecRK-I.8 is localized at the plasma membrane.
evidence: This is supported by the confocal microscopy data in Figure 3C showing colocalization with the plasma membrane marker AHA2.

claim: AHA2 encodes a plasma membrane localized P-type H+-ATPase.
source: Since AHA2 encodes a well-established plasma membrane localized P-type H+- ATPase (DeWitt et al., 1996), this result indicates that LecRK-I.8 is localized at the plasma membrane.
evidence: This is supported by a citation to DeWitt et al. (1996).

claim: The kinase domain of LecRK-I.8 possesses kinase activity.
source: This result indicates that LecRK-I.8 possesses kinase activity.
evidence: This is supported by the autoradiograph in Figure 4 showing autophosphorylation and phosphorylation of myelin basic protein.

claim: The LecRK-I.8KD protein exhibited a strong autophosphorylation activity.
source: As shown in the autoradiograph, the LecRK-I.8KD protein exhibited a strong autophosphorylation activity and also phosphorylated myelin basic protein, a substrate commonly used for in vitro kinase assays.
evidence: This is supported by the autoradiograph in Figure 4.

claim: The LecRK-I.8KD protein phosphorylated myelin basic protein.
source: As shown in the autoradiograph, the LecRK-I.8KD protein exhibited a strong autophosphorylation activity and also phosphorylated myelin basic protein, a substrate commonly used for in vitro kinase assays.
evidence: This is supported by the autoradiograph in Figure 4.

claim: A significant NAD+ binding activity was detected for the immunoprecipitated eLecRK-I.8-GFP protein.
source: A significant NAD+ binding activity was detected for the immunoprecipitated eLecRK-I.8-GFP protein, but not for the GFP protein immunoprecipitated from transgenic plants expressing GFP using the same antibody (Figure 5A), indicating that the NAD+ binding activity is likely specific to eLecRK-I.8.
evidence: This is supported by the binding assay data in Figure 5A.

claim: NAD+ binding activity was not detected for the GFP protein immunoprecipitated from transgenic plants expressing GFP.
source: A significant NAD+ binding activity was detected for the immunoprecipitated eLecRK-I.8-GFP protein, but not for the GFP protein immunoprecipitated from transgenic plants expressing GFP using the same antibody (Figure 5A), indicating that the NAD+ binding activity is likely specific to eLecRK-I.8.
evidence: This is supported by the binding assay data in Figure 5A.

claim: A specific NAD+ binding activity was detected for an eLecRK-I.8-HA-His fusion protein transiently expressed in N. benthamiana.
source: A specific NAD+ binding activity was also detected for an eLecRK-I.8-HA-His fusion protein transiently expressed in N. benthamiana (Figure 5B and Figure 5—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This is supported by the binding assay data in Figure 5B.

claim: NAD+ binding activity was detected for the recombinant fusion protein MBP-eLecRK-I.8.
source: Furthermore, NAD+ binding activity was detected for the recombinant fusion protein MBP-eLecRK-I.8 but not for MBP, MBP-eDORN1 (AAs 22 to 288), and MBP-eLecRK-I.3 (AAs 22 to 286) (Figure 5C and Figure 5—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: This is supported by the binding assay data in Figure 5C.

claim: NAD+ binding activity was not detected for MBP, MBP-eDORN1, and MBP-eLecRK-I.3.
source: Furthermore, NAD+ binding activity was detected for the recombinant fusion protein MBP-eLecRK-I.8 but not for MBP, MBP-eDORN1 (AAs 22 to 288), and MBP-eLecRK-I.3 (AAs 22 to 286) (Figure 5C and Figure 5—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: This is supported by the binding assay data in Figure 5C.

claim: The extracellular domain of LecRK-I.6 did not bind NAD+.
source: The extracellular domain of LecRK-I.6 (AAs 22 to 286), which is the closest homolog of LecRK-I.8 (Bouwmeester and Govers, 2009), did not bind NAD+, either (Figure 5—figure supplement 2), suggesting that LecRK-I.6 may not be an eNAD+ receptor.
evidence: This is supported by the binding assay data in Figure 5—figure supplement 2.

claim: LecRK-I.6 may not be an eNAD+ receptor.
source: The extracellular domain of LecRK-I.6 (AAs 22 to 286), which is the closest homolog of LecRK-I.8 (Bouwmeester and Govers, 2009), did not bind NAD+, either (Figure 5—figure supplement 2), suggesting that LecRK-I.6 may not be an eNAD+ receptor.
evidence: This is inferred from the lack of NAD+ binding to LecRK-I.6.

claim: Not all of the extracellular lectin domains of L-type LecRKs can bind NAD+.
source: Since LecRK-I.8, DORN1, LecRK-I.3, and LecRK-I.6, all are L-type LecRKs and belong to the LecRK-I clade (Bouwmeester and Govers, 2009), this result indicates that not all of the extracellular lectin domains of L-type LecRKs can bind NAD+.
evidence: This is inferred from the differential NAD+ binding among different L-type LecRKs.

claim: A dramatic increase of NAD+ binding activity was detected in the membrane fractions of the 35S:LecRK-I.8 transgenic plants.
source: In addition, we detected a dramatic increase of NAD+ binding activity in the membrane fractions of the 35S:LecRK-I.8 transgenic plants and a clear decrease of NAD+ binding activity in the membrane fractions of the lecrk-I.8–2 mutant plants (Figure 5D).
evidence: This is supported by the binding assay data in Figure 5D.

claim: A clear decrease of NAD+ binding activity was detected in the membrane fractions of the lecrk-I.8–2 mutant plants.
